**Given:** The two-auxiliary-leg RTT matrix relation with $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$ with the auxiliary flip $P_N(e_a\otimes e_b)=e_b\otimes e_a$, and $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$.



1.1 In the coefficient of the auxiliary row $(i,k)$ and column $(j,l)$, the $xI$ part of the left side is $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)$ and the $iP$ part is $i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)$, because the flip sends the row $(i,k)$ to $(k,i)$. On the right side the corresponding terms are $x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)$ and $i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$, since the flip acts on the column. Thus equality of those matrix entries gives $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)+i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)=x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)+i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Subtract the two $x$-terms and move the two $i$-terms to the other side. The result is exactly the displayed commutator relation. Conversely, if that relation holds for every four indices, the coefficient computation in step 1.1 makes every auxiliary matrix entry of the RTT difference zero, hence the full matrix relation holds. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, the RTT Yangian presentation, and the proposed maps above.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $T_0(u)=I+O(u^{-1})$ satisfies $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$, with proposed coproduct matrix product $\Delta(T_0(u))=T_0^{[1]}(u)T_0^{[2]}(u)$, counit $\epsilon(T_0(u))=I$, and antipode formula $S(T_0(u))=T_0(u)^{-1}$.



1.1 Each coefficient of $T^{[1]}(u)T^{[2]}(u)$ is a finite sum: the coefficient of $u^{-n}$ uses only the finitely many pairs of exponents adding to $n$ and the finite index sum $1\le k\le N$. Thus the proposed coproduct lands in the ordinary algebraic tensor product. For two independent Yangian factors, write $T_s^{[r]}$ for the matrix acting on auxiliary leg $s\in\{1,2\}$ and coefficient factor $r\in\{1,2\}$. Then $T_1^{[2]}$ commutes with $T_2^{[1]}$, and $T_1^{[1]}$ commutes with $T_2^{[2]}$, because each pair acts on disjoint tensor factors. Reordering these pairs and applying the RTT relation first in coefficient factor $1$ and then in factor $2$ gives $R_{12}T_1^{[1]}T_1^{[2]}T_2^{[1]}T_2^{[2]}=T_2^{[1]}T_2^{[2]}T_1^{[1]}T_1^{[2]}R_{12}$. The middle matrix product is precisely the RTT relation for $\Delta(T)$, so $\Delta$ preserves the defining relation and extends to a unital algebra homomorphism. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Iterating the matrix product yields $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(T)=T^{[1]}T^{[2]}T^{[3]}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(T)$, so the coproduct is coassociative coefficientwise. Substitution $T\mapsto I$ sends the RTT relation to $R=R$, so it defines a unital counit homomorphism; it also gives $(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(T)=T=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(T)$ and $\epsilon(1)=1$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $T(u)=I+O(u^{-1})$, recursively solving $T(u)T(u)^{-1}=I$ gives a unique right inverse; solving in the reverse order gives a left inverse, and associativity makes them equal. Each inverse coefficient is a finite polynomial in the coefficients of $T-I$, because only products of at most $n$ positive-degree terms contribute to $u^{-n}$. Write $A=T_1(u)$ and $B=T_2(v)$. In $RAB=BAR$, multiply on the left by $A^{-1}B^{-1}=(BA)^{-1}$ and on the right by $B^{-1}A^{-1}=(AB)^{-1}$ to obtain $A^{-1}B^{-1}R=RB^{-1}A^{-1}$. Define an anti-homomorphism on the free generator algebra by sending the coefficient matrix $T(u)$ entrywise to this inverse matrix. Applying it to the defining RTT relator reverses coefficient multiplication, so its image is $R B^{-1}A^{-1}=A^{-1}B^{-1}R$, exactly the same identity. Hence it preserves the RTT ideal and descends to the quotient, with $S(T(u))=T(u)^{-1}$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The two matrix inverse identities give $\sum_k S(t_{ik}(u))t_{kj}(u)=\delta_{ij}=\sum_k t_{ik}(u)S(t_{kj}(u))$, the left and right antipode identities on generators. For the left identity on a product $xy$, use $\Delta(xy)=\sum x_{(1)}y_{(1)}\otimes x_{(2)}y_{(2)}$ and anti-multiplicativity of $S$ to obtain $\sum S(y_{(1)})S(x_{(1)})x_{(2)}y_{(2)}=\epsilon(x)\sum S(y_{(1)})y_{(2)}=\epsilon(x)\epsilon(y)1$; the right identity follows from $\sum x_{(1)}y_{(1)}S(y_{(2)})S(x_{(2)})$. Induction on word length and linearity extend both identities to the generated algebra, giving $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=\eta\epsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $N\ge2$, the standard basis of $V_N$, and arbitrary $a,b,c\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $P_N(e_j\otimes e_k)=e_k\otimes e_j$, $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$, and $P_{ij}$ swaps the indicated tensor positions.

[F2] [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]]: on the ordered basis of $\mathbb C^2$, $P(e_j\otimes e_k)=e_k\otimes e_j$ and $R(x)=xI+iP$.

[F3] [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]]: for all complex spectral points, the corresponding un-checked three-leg operators satisfy the parameterized Yang–Baxter identity.



1.1 For $N=2$, the ordered basis and flip in [F1] are exactly those in [F2], so $R_2(x)=R(x)$ on the same $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$. The un-checked Yang–Baxter identity for this case is [F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 For $N\ge3$, put $s=P_{12}$, $t=P_{13}$, and $r=P_{23}$. Acting on any basis tensor $e_p\otimes e_q\otimes e_\ell$, the products $st,tr,rs$ all send $(p,q,\ell)$ to $(q,\ell,p)$, while $sr,rt,ts$ all send it to $(\ell,p,q)$; also $str=rts$ as both send $(p,q,\ell)$ to $(\ell,q,p)$. Hence, as operators, with $A=st=tr=rs$ and $B=sr=rt=ts$, those permutation identities hold on the whole basis. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 The flip satisfies $P_N^2=I$, so direct multiplication gives $(xI+iP_N)(xI-iP_N)=(x^2+1)I=(xI-iP_N)(xI+iP_N)$. Over $\mathbb C$, $x^2+1\ne0$ exactly when $x\notin\{i,-i\}$; division by this scalar gives the stated inverse. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Expanding the left side gives $xyzI+i(yz\,s+xy\,t+xz\,r)-(y\,st+z\,sr+x\,tr)-i\,str$; the right side gives $xyzI+i(yz\,s+xy\,t+xz\,r)-(x\,rt+z\,rs+y\,ts)-i\,rts$. By step 1.2, the quadratic parts are respectively $-((x+y)A+zB)$ and $-(zA+(x+y)B)$, which agree since $x+y=z$; the scalar and linear parts match termwise and the cubic terms match by $str=rts$. This proves the Yang–Baxter identity for all $N\ge3$, and step 1.1 covers $N=2$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The operators $P_+=(I+P_N)/2$ and $P_-=(I-P_N)/2$ are complementary projectors because $P_N^2=I$. Their images have bases $e_j\otimes e_j$, $e_j\otimes e_k+e_k\otimes e_j$ and $e_j\otimes e_k-e_k\otimes e_j$ for $j<k$, respectively, so their dimensions are $N(N+1)/2$ and $N(N-1)/2$. On these subspaces $R_N(x)$ acts by $x+i$ and $x-i$; therefore at $x=i$ it has kernel $\operatorname{im}P_-=\bigwedge^2V_N$, and at $x=-i$ it has kernel $\operatorname{im}P_+=\operatorname{Sym}^2V_N$, with the ranks stated. [given, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎



Each arrow is a composite endomorphism of $V_N^{\otimes3}$, with its rightmost factor applied first. The diagram records the two sides of the equation just proved; the equality follows from the basis-permutation calculation in the proof, not from the diagram.
